title: Alodia
capsule: Alodia (also Alwa) was a Christian Nubian kingdom centered on the capital Soba, situated near the confluence of the Blue and White Nile rivers south of modern Khartoum, and is attested from at least the mid-sixth century AD when it accepted Monophysite Christianity under Justinianic missionary influence. At its apex between roughly the eighth and eleventh centuries, Alodia was the largest and most southerly of the three Nubian Christian kingdoms, extending control over a broad swath of the central Sudanese savanna and reportedly maintaining a cavalry force and stone-built urban centers described favorably by Arab geographers such as Ibn Hawqal. Its decline was gradual, linked to the southward advance of Arab nomads and the spread of Islam; the Funj Sultanate, founded by a coalition of Arab and African groups, overran Soba around 1504–1506, ending Alodia's existence as a political entity.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Territorial extent is poorly documented; boundaries are reconstructed from Arab geographical descriptions, sparse archaeological surveys, and the general distribution of Nubian Christian material culture — the polygon should be treated as broadly approximate rather than precisely delineated.
